Abnoba.json.text: Abnoba is a Celtic goddess honoured in Britain and on the mainland. She gave her name to rivers called Avon, as the one in England that runs through Stratford. Rome called the Black Forest Mons Abnoba in her honor, and streams from its eastern slopes meet to form the young river Danube. A stone statue from Mühlburg shows her dressed as Diana, touching a tree while a hound and a hare rest beneath. A relief at the source of the Brigach adds a stag and a bird to her company. The hare ties her to the same ritual world as the goddess Andraste. Inscriptions from Muhlbach and Rothenburg keep her name, and a bronze native Diana in Köln may show her or the goddess Arduinna. Pliny and Tacitus both name her in their writings. Her image shows a huntress, her hunting dog, and a stag beside her.

Andraste.json.text: Andraste is a British goddess, also written Andrasta. The historian Cassius Dio preserves the only surviving account of her, and he says the name meant victory. The form looks like a feminine name built on a verb that carries the Celtic negative prefix an-, so it may suggest the unconquerable one. The warrior queen Boudicca of the Iceni called on her during the rising of ad 61. In the rite Boudicca freed a hare from among the folds of her garment, and the way it ran told the warriors the attack held favor. In her speech she hailed the goddess as one woman to another and asked for triumph, life, and freedom. Dio adds that the goddess was worshipped in a grove, a nemeton, where Roman women were put to death during the revolt. The hare was an occasional symbol of the warrior queen Medb, famed in Ireland. It turns fierce when caught, and so it fits an image of defense. Boudicca came close to driving the Romans from her land. When the war turned against her, she died by her own hand rather than face the humiliations the Romans gave their defeated enemies.

Annwn.json.text: Annwn, also called Annwyn and Annwfn, is the Welsh Otherworld, the Un-world that lies on the far side of ordinary life. Its name may grow from the old Celtic word dwfn, deep. A Gaulish inscription from Collias invokes underworld spirits with the word andounnabo, set at a ritual spring. The Welsh, like the Irish, offered several places for the Otherworld. Annwn means abyss. The Welsh saw it as a castle by the sea, called Caer Siddi. They also saw it as a court of intoxication, called Caer Feddwid, and as a palace of glass, called Caer Wydyr. Like Tir na nOg, that Irish island of the blessed, Annwn was a land of sweetness and charm. Its people knew neither age nor suffering. A magic cauldron fed each of them their fill. An unfailing well quenched their thirst. Two kings ruled Annwn, Arawn and Hafgan, locked in endless war. The legends tell more of Arawn. In the Mabinogi's first branch, the prince Pwyll met Arawn while hunting, and the two traded shapes for a year. That season bound the royal house of Dyfed to the powers of Annwfn. In the early poem Preiddiau Annwfn, which tells of the spoils of Annwn, Arthur and his men stormed stronghold after stronghold in that other realm.

Arawn.json.text: Arawn is a Welsh god. He is the lord of Annwn, the Welsh Otherworld. His world is a typical Celtic Otherworld. It is beautiful and unchanging, without pain, death, or disease. Its residents pass their time in merrymaking and games. Koch calls him the king of Annwfn in the Mabinogi's opening branch. Arawn owned a magical cauldron. It suggests a parallel with the Dagda, the Irish father god. Arawn had magical pigs, another motif of the Dagda. He handed the pigs to the mortal king Pryderi as a gift. The theft cost Gwydion his freedom, and Annwn held him prisoner after he took the pigs. Three magical animals of Arawn were stolen by the obscure god Amaethon. The motif holds that domesticated animals once belonged to the gods. People had to bring them to this world by force or trickery. In the Mabinogi tale of Pwyll, Arawn exchanged identities with the mortal king for a year. Pwyll spent his year in the Otherworld and killed Arawn's enemy and rival, Hafgan. Koch adds a rule to that combat. A single blow could kill Hafgan, but a second blow gave him back his strength. So the victor had to strike once and stop. Pwyll learned the rule and ended the long war in one stroke. In return Arawn built a model kingdom in Dyfed, known for warmth, kindness, and a clear sense of justice. An early poem about the spoils of Annwfn still remembers the king and his realm.

Arberth.json.text: Arberth is a Welsh mythological site. Pwyll's kingdom held the mound, a place of fairy magic that bore this name. Koch identifies it with Narberth in Pembrokeshire and calls it the royal seat of the old kingdom of Dyfed. People went there to see visions. The mound itself bears the name Gorsedd Arberth, and strange events gather around it. It is the scene of much of the Mabinogi, standing at the heart of the first and fourth branches. The mystifying horsewoman Rhiannon appears on the mound in Pwyll's tale. Her horse appears to walk, yet no one can catch her. In the tale of Manawydan, a mist descends on the mound and takes the people of Dyfed away.

Armorica.json.text: Armorica is an ancient place-name. It names the coast of Gaul facing the Atlantic. The name means country facing the sea. In Roman usage the Tractus Armoricanus ran from the mouth of the Seine to the Loire. The tract took in the country of the Belgae to the west and the Aquitani to the north, land that Normandy and Brittany later shared. Julius Caesar gives the earliest surviving examples of the name. He writes of the civitates Armoricae, the tribal states by the ocean. His list names the Curiosolites, the Redones, the Ambibarii, the Caletes, the Osismii, the Veneti, the Lemovices, and the Venelli. Caesar also records the Veneti as the strongest people of the coast and tells how Rome broke their sea power. Their name lives on in Breton Gwened, the town the French call Vannes. Modern works often use Armorica for the land later called Brittany. Koch also records the older spelling Aremorica.

banshee.json.text: The banshee is an Irish spirit of death. The name means the woman of the fairy people. In an older age she was the goddess of a land and of its sovereignty. Koch traces her to the territorial goddesses of early Irish literature, who guarded their rulers and could also appear as war goddesses under the name Badb. When her glory faded, her role narrowed to a single task. She now warns that death draws near. She favors the old families of Ireland. Their names often begin with O or Mac. She appears as a hag or as a young woman. She is most often an outdoor being in a white cloak, with her head bare. Red hair and white or green robes mark her as other. She wails, and she draws a golden comb through her hair. In the east of Ireland she combs that hair, and in Galway she washes a garment in a stream. That deed matches the bean-nighe of Gaelic Scotland and the kannerezed noz of Brittany. An older layer of the same image shows the war goddess badhbh washing the clothes of men fated to fall in battle. A Galway tale places such a washer by the stream on the eve of Aughrim in 1691. The sovereignty goddess could also foretell a king's death. Aoibheall of Craglea foretold the fall of Brian Bóruma at Clontarf in 1014. In the eighth-century Táin Bó Fraích, the cries of Otherworld women, led by the hero's own mother Bé Find, sang Fraoch toward his end. Áine of north Munster appears as a weeping banshee and the ancestress of the FitzGeralds. She warns of death from any cause. The Washer at the Ford warns only of a death in battle. A banshee can follow her own people when they travel. The banshee of the O'Gradys family went with them to Canada.

Balor.json.text: Balor is an Irish god. He is also called Balar, Bolar, and Balor of the Evil Eye. He reigned as king of the Fomorians, the monstrous race who held Ireland before the first invaders. His daughter was the fair Eithne. A prophecy warned that a son born to Eithne would kill his grandfather. Balor shut Eithne in a tower to keep every man away from her. He hoped that this would spare his own life. Koch takes his fullest early portrait of him from the second battle at Mag Tuired. That tale was set down in the ninth or tenth century. There Balor leads the Fomoiri against his grandson Lug and the Tuath Dé. Balor's greed undid his plan. He stole the magical cow Glas Ghaibhleann from a smith. Lugh struck him down in that battle with a slingshot or a spear made by the smith god Goibniu. Lugh cut off Balor's head. Even in death, Balor's remaining eye could split boulders. The eye was his ruin from the start. Koch tells how Balor won the eye as a boy, spying on his father's druids at their magic. Its heavy lid took four men to lift, and its gaze struck soldiers of the Tuath Dé helpless. When Lug's stone flew through it, the fatal power turned back on the Fomoiri. Monaghan calls the eye a third eye set at the centre of Balor's forehead. It spat flames and destruction. His consort Cethlion carried poisons of her own, and they killed the god Dagda. In later folk-tales Balor loses his role as a war leader and becomes a monstrous villain. Scholars see him in two lights: a sun god, or a clash between the outgoing year and the one arriving. The tale ties him to the Hebrides, and modern storytellers place his fortress on Tory Island. He is linked to Mizen Head in County Cork and to Land's End in Wales.

Banba.json.text: Banba is an Irish goddess. She is one of three earth goddesses, with Fódla and Ériu, who met the Milesians. The medieval lore of women and the Book of Invasions group the three as daughters of Fiachra or of Ernmas. The Milesians were the mythological invaders seen as the first Irish Celts. The Book of Invasions places the meeting at Slieve Mis in County Kerry. Some sources place her on the plain from which the hill of Tara rises. Banba offered the Milesians happiness and wealth if the land bore her name. The Milesians instead gave precedence to Ériu, who made the same promise from the hill of Uisneach. The sources name a god or hero for each goddess as her husband. Banba's husband was Mac Cuill, whose name means son of Hazel. Legend holds that the salmon of wisdom fed on hazel nuts. Koch calls Mac Cuill a king of the Tuath Dé and a grandson of the Dagda. Geoffrey Keating, drawing on a lost Old Irish manuscript, tells another arrival tale. In that telling Banba and her sisters arrived as daughters of Cain, fifty women and three men with them. All of them died in a plague. The name may join ban, woman, with ba, an old word for death, for gain, or for cow. That last sense echoes Bóand, the river Boyne, whose name means white as a cow. The pig is an emblem of Banba, and her name resembles the Irish word for piglet, banb. Banba said she had walked Ireland before the time of the biblical Noah. In some tellings the Milesians drove her out with sung spells. Her name survives today as a poetic name for Ireland.

Bath.json.text: Bath is a British mythological site. It lies in the southwest of England, where the river Avon cuts through the limestone of the Cotswolds. Three hot springs rise within a short walk of one another. People have valued these waters as a cure for roughly two thousand years. Some think the spring was used before the Celts. Coins from the late Iron Age and the remains of a causeway have come to light beneath the later King's Bath. The records that survive date from Celtic times. The local goddess was Sulis, and the Romans named the town Aquae Sulis, the waters of Sulis. The Romans folded Sul into their goddess Minerva. They raised columned temples and inner bathing rooms. Koch dates the first sanctuary complex to the Flavian age, between ad 69 and 138. It held a Corinthian temple of four columns, a paved court, an altar, and a spring left open to the sky. A fort on the Fosse Way watched the river crossing in the first years of the conquest. After the army moved on, the town grew as a civil settlement around the crossing. These buildings stand today. Celtic custom showed itself at Bath. People threw coins into the water. They also wrote curses on sheets of lead. Excavators have found 16,000 coins at the site. They have found more than 50 cursing tablets as well.

Badb.json.text: Badb, also written Bodb, means the scald crow. In early Irish tradition she was a supernatural woman linked to battle and slaughter. The name works as a proper name and as a general term for a battle creature. She sometimes merges with the Morrigan, Nemain, Be Neit, or Macha, and at other times stands apart from them. The stock phrase badb catha means the Badb of battle. Translators of Latin tales recast the Furies and Bellona as fern battle goddesses named Badb. Her appearance was an evil omen. The male figure Bodb Derg, king of the sidhe of Munster, shared her name.

boar.json.text: The wild boar held deep symbolic weight for the ancient Celts. Art and coinage from the Continent and the islands show it. Writers linked the Gaulish god Moccus to the Roman Mercury, and he may have stood for a pig or a boar. In the Welsh tale Culhwch and Olwen, Arthur's men first hunted Ysgithrwyn, a chief boar called the white tusk, before the great chase of Twrch Trwyth and his offspring. The Middle Welsh name hob set the tame pig's origin in the Otherworld. In the Fourth Branch of the Mabinogi, a sow from the Otherworld guided Gwydion to the slain Lleu.

aisling.json.text: An aisling is a vision poem in the Irish language, often allegorical and usually written in the eighteenth century. In it a woman from the Otherworld visits the poet in a dream. Gerard Murphy set out three principal forms. The love aisling bewitches the poet with the woman's beauty. The prophecy aisling lets the dreamer predict the future. In the allegorical aisling the woman often stands for Ireland and comforts the distressed poet. Murphy thought the third form, common in the eighteenth century, might fuse the first two. The early Irish Aislinge Oengusa, the vision of Aonghus, and the later Aislinge Meic Con Glinne are famous examples.
